text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, poultry housing should protect birds from heat, heavy rain, predators, rodents, wild birds, and disease exposure while allowing good airflow. During the wet season (roughly May–October), main concerns are wet litter, mud, poor drainage, contaminated water, and reduced ventilation if the house is closed to keep out rain. During the dry season (roughly November–April), heat, dust, dehydration, and inadequate airflow matter more. Avoid overcrowding, which increases stress, contamination, and disease transmission — there is no single universal stocking-density number since it depends on species, age, system, ventilation, and climate. Biosecurity means reducing contact between domestic birds and wild birds, newly purchased poultry, neighboring flocks, contaminated equipment, and visiting people. New birds should be kept separate for a veterinary-guided period before mixing; sick birds should be separated promptly; dead birds should be removed safely and not left accessible to other animals. For smallholders with free-ranging birds, complete separation from wild birds/neighboring flocks may be unrealistic — the chatbot should not pretend otherwise, and should instead recommend reducing unnecessary contact around feed, water, and nighttime housing. Sudden mortality or rapidly spreading respiratory/neurological disease is an urgent warning sign requiring reduced movement and veterinary/animal-health investigation — never diagnosed from symptoms alone. No specific chicken or duck breed is claimed as predominant in Preah Vihear without reliable evidence.
